title: Channel Home Centers, Division of Grace Retail Corp. v. Grossman
lead: A developer promises exclusive negotiations in a detailed letter of intent, then leases to a competitor while the first tenant is preparing the final papers.

actors.name: Channel Home Centers
actors.role: Home-improvement retailer seeking an anchor lease and enforcement of a preliminary negotiation promise.

actors.name: Frank Grossman and sons
actors.role: Developers controlling the mall-acquisition and leasing entities.

actors.name: Baker Investment Corporation and Equitable Life Assurance
actors.role: Equitable owner and legal-title holder during negotiations.

actors.name: Mr. Good Buys
actors.role: Competing retailer that later obtained the lease.

proceedings: The District Court converted a brief preliminary-injunction hearing into a final trial without advance notice and entered judgment against Channel.
Channel did not use a later opportunity for another hearing or request further time and discovery, waiving that procedural objection.
The Third Circuit reversed on the preliminary-contract analysis and remanded for a full trial.
limits: The letter was conceded not to be a completed lease. The decision permits a finding of a narrower negotiation contract and leaves actual intent and the disputed deadline for trial; it awards no possession or damages.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Channel considers an anchor location in a struggling mall
sections.cue: Why did Grossman want a signed letter?
paragraphs: Channel operated home-improvement stores and considered Cedarbrook Mall in Cheltenham Township near Philadelphia. Frank Grossman and his sons controlled entities acquiring and leasing the property. Baker Investment was equitable owner, Equitable Life held title, and closing was anticipated in February 1985. Rehabilitation and new tenants were meant to revive the mall, with Channel as a fourth anchor helping financing prospects.

After a November 28, 1984 tour, Grossman asked for a letter he could show banks and others. Channel signed a detailed December 11 letter, and Grossman signed and returned it. It described roughly 70,400 square feet, a twenty-five-year term, stepped and percentage rent, renewals, taxes, maintenance, and landlord work. A mutually satisfactory final lease remained subject to parent-company approval, title, and sign permits or variances. Prelease expenditures were expressly at the spender’s risk.

To induce Channel to proceed, Grossman promised to remove the store from the market and negotiate only the described transaction to completion. That narrower commitment, not a final lease, became Channel’s asserted contract.

sources.pinpoint: Proposed anchor and letter; 795 F.2d at 292–294 & n.2,298–301

sections.title: Both sides prepare for a lease while a rival appears
sections.cue: What remained disputed about the deadline?
paragraphs: Channel directed its parent’s lawyers to draft, obtained its own real-estate committee approval, measured, planned marketing and construction, arranged deliveries, and bought materials or equipment. Its submissions indicated about $25,000 spent. The developers sought sign zoning permission. These acts supported intent without conclusively establishing either contract.

On January 11 Channel’s lawyer sent a forty-one-page draft and requested exhibit documents. The developers supplied title and site material January 16, reporting work had begun, and anticipated prompt execution in a January 17 letter. A January 23 call addressed a use clause and another conference; the parties later disputed who had to arrange it.

Mr. Good Buys contacted Grossman around January 22 and toured on January 25. On February 6 Grossman declared Channel negotiations over for failure to deliver a signed acceptable lease within thirty days. The letter had no such limit. Grossman testified to an oral draft deadline; Channel officers denied any finite deadline, and February 6 supplied its first written mention. On February 7 he leased to the competitor at substantially greater base rent, though without Channel’s proposed percentage rent. Channel’s parent approved its proposed lease February 13.

sources.pinpoint: Performance and competing tenant; 795 F.2d at 294–296 & n.3

sections.title: A ten-minute preliminary hearing unexpectedly becomes final
sections.cue: Why did the procedural error not itself produce reversal?
paragraphs: Channel sued in diversity in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania on February 15 for breach and preliminary relief. A temporary restraining order protected its position until a February 25 hearing lasting about ten minutes and mostly involving limited depositions. Without advance notice, the judge consolidated it with trial under Rule 65(a)(2), denied relief, and on March 26 entered judgment against Channel for lack of intent, consideration, and compliance with the lease statute of frauds.

Channel sought reconsideration, explaining its need for discovery about financing and other anchors. On May 7 the judge adhered to judgment but offered another hearing if requested within fifteen days. Channel did not request it or ask for more discovery or time in response. The Third Circuit condemned the lack of clear advance consolidation notice but held the later inaction waived that objection. Reversal rested elsewhere.

sources.pinpoint: Premature judgment and waiver; 795 F.2d at 296–298

sections.title: The court identifies the preliminary promise as a separate contract
sections.cue: Why did failure to form a lease not resolve the case?
paragraphs: Becker wrote for himself, Weis, and Higginbotham. With no square Pennsylvania decision, the panel predicted that an express agreement to negotiate could be enforced if intent, definiteness, and consideration were established. It did not create a universal precontractual good-faith duty or conflate it with good faith in performing an existing contract.

Channel conceded that the letter did not complete a lease. The lease statute of frauds therefore did not answer the narrower obligation to withdraw the premises and negotiate exclusively in good faith. Final approvals and unfinished terms did not necessarily defeat that promise.

The explicit language, detailed subject, reciprocal preparations, and communications supported a finding of intended preliminary obligation. They did not compel it; conflicting evidence still required a factfinder.

sections.title: The requested letter can supply consideration without a cash payment
sections.cue: What issues did the remand leave for trial?
paragraphs: Grossman wanted a serious anchor tenant’s written interest to help obtain permanent financing. Channel, knowing that purpose, tendered the requested letter in return for exclusivity. That bargained-for benefit could be consideration without payment or proof that a bank actually lent on the letter. The theory did not rest solely on expenditures, and the court did not reach unilateral-contract or promissory-estoppel alternatives.

The Third Circuit found a sufficiently definite negotiation promise and evidence of consideration and reversed for a full trial, encouraging expedited further discovery. Actual binding intent remained disputed. So did the alleged thirty-day term: if Channel agreed to deliver a draft by then and failed, exclusivity could have ended; otherwise a reasonable time depended on context. Other formation questions remained open.
Channel obtained an opportunity to prove its preliminary contract, not specific performance of a completed lease, possession, or a damages award.

sources.pinpoint: Consideration; Holding and limits; 795 F.2d at 297 n.6,300–301 & n.10
